description: We're a full team of friends who work well together. Between us we cover machine learning, computer vision, full-stack development, design, research, science, and data analysis. We like learning by solving real problems, an idea Elon Musk has talked about, and we figure things out as we go. For Dancing with the SARs, we want to use data analysis, ML, and computer vision to make SAR data easier to work with in a simple interface.
summary:
Long-duration space missions to the Moon and Mars introduce a major medical challenge: communication delays with Earth can reach up to 20 minutes each way. If an astronaut experiences an acute stress episode or panic attack, ground-based Flight Surgeons cannot intervene in real time. At the same time, standard wearable monitors often fail to tell the difference between a high heart rate caused by daily physical exercise and one caused by psychological distress.

We built AstroSync to solve this problem right on board the spacecraft. Our system combines two main parts: a machine learning model and an interactive AI companion. First, we trained a Random Forest classifier on 40,000+ physiological sensor data windows (heart rate, heart rate variability, skin sweat conductivity, skin temperature, and 3-axis movement) using 29 engineered features. The model separates Acute Stress from Aerobic and Anaerobic exercise with 97.05% accuracy and a 0.988 ROC-AUC score. Second, we wrote a Python script that passes the model's live predictions and vital signs directly into a chatbot built on Gradio. When the model detects high stress, the chatbot immediately starts a supportive conversation based on the astronaut's actual readings and walks them through breathing exercises to calm down.
details:
How AstroSync Works?

We designed AstroSync as a two-part closed-loop pipeline that monitors astronaut vitals and steps in when stress levels spike:

- Data Windowing and Feature Engineering: We took raw wearable signals—Heart Rate (HR), Inter-Beat Interval (IBI/HRV), Electrodermal Activity (EDA), Skin Temperature (TEMP), and 3-Axis Accelerometer (ACC)—and split them into 30-second rolling windows with a 5-second shift. Across these 40,000 windows, we calculated 29 physiological features, including custom ratios like the Cardio Load Index (which separates heart rate spikes from physical body movement), Autonomic Stress Index, and Sympathetic Arousal.

- Machine Learning Classification: To mimic how NASA calibrates baseline vitals for a specific crew before launch, we used Stratified 5-Fold Cross-Validation across 40,000+ windows. We tested 7 different algorithms (Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost) and tuned the top performers using RandomizedSearchCV. Our final Random Forest model classifies the crew member's state into Class 0 (Acute Stress), Class 1 (Aerobic Exercise), or Class 2 (Anaerobic Exercise).

- Connecting the Model to the Chatbot: Instead of leaving the ML model as a silent dashboard, we connected its live output to a conversational agent. A Python function pulls a sample from the test set, runs the Random Forest prediction, identifies which vital signs triggered the alert (for example, high EDA sweat combined with low physical motion), and passes those exact numbers into the system prompt of our AI Companion. The chatbot then talks to the astronaut using their real vitals and guides them through a 4-4-4 box-breathing routine.

 

2. Why It Matters & Key Benefits

- Works During Comms Blackouts: Gives astronauts immediate psychological support without waiting 20 minutes for a reply from Earth.

- Cuts Down False Alarms: Astronauts exercise heavily every day to prevent bone and muscle loss. By separating exercise from stress, our model stops normal workouts from triggering false medical alerts.

- Useful on Earth Too: The exact same setup can help monitor ICU patients, commercial pilots, or workers in isolated environments like offshore rigs.

 

3. Tools and Coding Stack

- Language: Python 3 (developed and tested on Google Colab)

- Data & ML Libraries: Pandas, NumPy, Scikit-learn, Joblib (for saving the compressed model)

- Interface & Chatbot: Gradio (for the web dashboard) and G4F LLM Client

 

4. What Works Right Now in Our Prototype

- Our trained Random Forest model achieves 98.05% test accuracy, 0.9988 multi-class ROC-AUC, and a 98.40% F1-score on the Acute Stress class (97.36% Precision, 99.46% Recall).

- Our Gradio web app is live and functional: clicking "Run ML Model on New Sample" pulls real sensor data, shows the predicted state and confidence score, and updates the chatbot's context immediately.

 

5. Current Limitations & Our Future Roadmap

- Current Limitations: Right now, our dataset comes from Earth-based stress and exercise sessions. In actual microgravity, bodily fluids shift toward the head, which changes an astronaut's baseline heart rate over time. Also, our current prototype reads from saved test windows and interacts through text rather than hardware headsets.

- What We Plan to Build Next:

  1. Bio-Adaptive VR Environments: We plan to link our ML model's output directly to Virtual Reality (VR) headsets using Unity/WebXR. When stress probability crosses 60%, the headset will open a calming Earth nature scene where lighting, sound, and breathing visuals adjust automatically as the astronaut's heart rate and skin conductance drop.

  2. Offline Voice AI & Vocal Stress Detection: Running a small, quantized language model locally on the spacecraft's computers so it works 100% offline, while adding voice tone analysis to spot stress from how the astronaut speaks.

  3. In-Flight Microgravity Recalibration: Adding continual on-device learning so the model updates each astronaut's baseline vitals week by week as their body adapts to space.

  4. Direct Bluetooth Wearable Streaming: Connecting the code directly to smartwatches or biometric shirts (like Astroskin) via Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) instead of reading pre-recorded files.

  5. Delayed Flight Surgeon Reports: Packaging short, automated medical summaries of any stress event and how the astronaut recovered, ready to send to NASA doctors on Earth as soon as the communication window reopens.
